alt: Paper 1 combines translation from Urdu into English, reading comprehension in Urdu, and an extended Urdu response to an independent research question. Each rewards different preparation, and translation and free writing pull in opposite directions.
caption: Three distinct skills: revise them as separate strands.

alt: Three versions of one Urdu sentence: literal ("On him anger came", unnatural), too free ("He lost his temper", loses register) and balanced ("He became angry", accurate and natural), with three checks: nothing omitted, natural English, register preserved.
caption: Aim between literal and free: everything present, natural, and in the same register.

alt: What-questions want located detail, why-questions want inference, and questions on the writer’s attitude want evidence of tone such as word choice, irony and emphasis. Use your own words, match length to marks, and look around a phrase for its meaning.
caption: Name the question type first: detail, inference or tone.

alt: Section C is worth 40 marks for about 320 to 370 words: AO4 knowledge and understanding of society and culture via research (20), AO2 use of the unseen text (10) and AO3 accuracy and range of language (10). Research covers all three aspects of one subject in one country or area, and a planned structure prevents drift.
caption: Half the essay marks come from your research; plan before you write.

alt: Five recurring accuracy features for extended Urdu writing: gender agreement across noun, adjective and verb; consistent tense and person; postpositions, especially the ergative with transitive perfective verbs; izafat in formal register; and accurate script.
caption: Leave time to check agreement, postpositions and script.
